OG-10.from: Every square metre of roof catches approximately 1 litre of water per millimetre of rainfall. A 150m² roof in a region with 1,000mm annual rainfall can harvest 150,000 litres per year. This planner helps you size your system correctly.
OG-10.to: Every square metre of roof catches about 1 litre of water per millimetre of rainfall, before losses. Worked example, not your figure: a 150m² roof where 1,000mm of rain falls in a year catches about 150,000 litres before losses. Use your own roof area and your own local rainfall below. Rainwater from a roof is not automatically safe to drink. If you want to use it for drinking or other household uses it has to be treated, and some councils also require testing — check your council's requirements before you start.
OG-10.reason: The 150,000 L figure ignored losses and read as a promise; it becomes a labelled worked example, 'before losses'. Adds that roof water is not automatically drinkable: MBIE — it must be treated for drinking or other household use, and some councils require testing.

OG-10.from:
Annual Harvest (L) = Roof Area (m²) × Annual Rainfall (mm) × Efficiency (%)
Efficiency accounts for evaporation, overflow, and first-flush diversion. 85–90% is typical for a well-designed system.
OG-10.to:
Annual Harvest (L) = Roof Area (m²) × Annual Rainfall (mm) × Efficiency (%)
One square metre of roof catches one litre per millimetre of rain, so the first two numbers give the water that lands on the roof. Efficiency is what you actually capture after evaporation, overflow, gutter losses and first-flush diversion — there is no standard figure: ask your supplier or installer what allowance suits your roof, gutters and first-flush device. For annual rainfall, use local figures for your area from your regional council or NIWA.
OG-10.reason: '85–90% is typical' is an unsourced rule of thumb: no NZ or AU official source read gives a collection-efficiency figure. Explains what efficiency means and sends the member to their supplier or installer. Rainfall: local figures (regional council, NIWA).

OG-10.from: How many litres does your household use per day? (Typical NZ home: 150–300L/day)
OG-10.to: How many litres does your household use per day? Use your own figure — your water bill or meter if you have one, or a supplier's estimate for a household your size.

OG-10.from: How many days without rain do you want to cover? (Recommended: 21–30 days minimum)
OG-10.to: How many days without rain do you want to cover? Choose a length that suits your area — local rainfall records show how long dry spells usually last where you live.
OG-10.reason: 'Recommended: 21–30 days minimum' is an unsourced universal rule.

OG-10.from: Tank Size (L) = Daily Use × Dry Spell Days
OG-10.to:
Tank Size (L) = Daily Use × Dry Spell Days
This is the minimum to cover that dry spell with no rain at all. What you can actually keep in the tank also depends on your roof area and rainfall (Step 1).
OG-10.reason: Makes the assumption visible: the formula ignores refill during the period.

OG-10.from:
Tank Size Reality

Most households underestimate tank size. A 1,000L tank sounds big but only covers 3–7 days for a typical home. For genuine water independence, think in multiples of 5,000L or 10,000L. Two smaller tanks are often better than one giant — redundancy matters.
OG-10.to:
Tank Size Reality

Tank size depends on your roof area, your local rainfall, what you will use the water for and whether you also have mains water. Building Performance (MBIE) guidance: for garden watering, a rain barrel (generally about 240 litres) or a tank of 500 litres plus; for indoor supply you need a larger tank — in areas with year-round rain a 5,000-litre tank provides a good proportion of household use, and with dry summers 10,000 litres plus; if rainwater is your only water supply, at least 30,000 litres. Talk to local suppliers about the size that suits your climate and household. Two smaller tanks can give redundancy that one large tank cannot.
OG-10.reason: Removes the unsourced '1,000L covers 3–7 days' and 'multiples of 5,000L or 10,000L'. Replaced with MBIE's published NZ guidance (240 L barrel / 500 L+ garden; 5,000 L year-round rain; 10,000 L+ dry summers; at least 30,000 L if rainwater is the only supply).

OG-10.from:
Tank Size Reality

Most households underestimate tank size. A 1,000L tank sounds big but only covers 3–7 days for a typical home. For genuine water independence, think in multiples of 5,000L or 10,000L. Two smaller tanks are often better than one giant — redundancy matters.
OG-10.to:

OG-10.from: Total system estimated cost
OG-10.to:
Total system estimated cost

A rainwater system that supplies the house needs a pump. Connecting it to household plumbing is work for a qualified plumber — including the backflow prevention device where there is also a mains supply — and the pump's fixed electrical work is for a licensed electrical worker.
OG-10.reason: PLUMBING/ELECTRICAL: the component list includes a pressure pump and household supply, with no mention of who may do the work. MBIE: a system supplying the house needs a pump; a backflow prevention device must be installed by a qualified plumber. NZ electrical term (WorkSafe NZ).

OG-10.from: Council consent required? (Check local rules — many areas exempt under certain sizes)
OG-10.to: Council requirements checked? (Rules differ by council. Connecting rainwater to the plumbing of a house that also has mains water needs a building consent, and the law requires the mains supply to be isolated by a backflow prevention device installed by a qualified plumber. A tank on a stand over one metre high generally needs a consent too.)
OG-10.reason: REGULATORY: 'many areas exempt under certain sizes' is an invented compliance claim. MBIE: rules differ by council; connecting to the plumbing of a house with mains water needs a building consent and a backflow prevention device installed by a qualified plumber; a tank on a stand over one metre high generally needs a consent.

OG-10.to: Council, state and territory requirements checked? (Rules differ by area — contact your local council about building or planning rules for rainwater tanks, and ask a licensed plumber about connecting to household plumbing.)
OG-10.reason: REGULATORY: requirements vary by council, state and territory. NSW Health directs people to their local council for building or planning rules. No national rule is claimed.

OG-10.from:
Tank Placement Rules

1. On stable, level ground — concrete pad recommended
2. Close to downpipes to minimise pipe runs
3. Dark location or opaque tank — sunlight grows algae
4. Above garden / irrigation if gravity-feeding
5. Accessible for cleaning and maintenance
OG-10.to:
Tank Placement Rules

1. On stable, level ground — concrete pad recommended
2. Close to downpipes to minimise pipe runs
3. Dark location or opaque tank — many tanks are dark-coloured to stop light getting in and encouraging algae
4. Above garden / irrigation if gravity-feeding
5. Accessible for cleaning and maintenance
6. Screen the tank inlet to keep out insects, birds and animals, and keep the tank tightly covered
7. Overflow has to be contained on your property or directed to the stormwater system — overflow that damages your property or a neighbour's can leave you liable
OG-10.reason: Keeps the practical points and grounds the algae one in MBIE's wording. Adds inlet screening and MBIE's overflow rule (contain on your property or direct to stormwater; damage can leave you liable).
